title: Normal empirical rule 68-95-99.7 approximation versus exact table values
scenario_markdown: A precision machining center manufactures roller bearing outer diameters with specifications normally distributed around mean $\mu = 100\text{ mm}$ with standard deviation $\sigma = 15\text{ mm}$ ($X \sim N(100, 15^2)$). A quality assurance engineer evaluates the proportion of bearings falling within two standard deviations of the mean ($[\mu - 2\sigma, \mu + 2\sigma] = [70\text{ mm}, 130\text{ mm}]$), comparing the 68–95–99.7 Empirical Rule against exact cumulative normal probabilities.
assumptions: Continuous normal distribution X ~ N(100, 15^2) in mm

approval.notes: Reviewed empirical rule comparison: Empirical Rule states approximately 95% within 2 standard deviations. Exact normal probability is Phi(2.00) - Phi(-2.00) = 0.97725 - 0.02275 = 0.9545 (95.45%). Explored bell-shaped symmetry condition versus Chebyshev inequality. Excel formulas verified.
approval.delegation_basis: Content backlog Batch 1: Row 3.2 normal distribution expansion

stages.prompt_markdown: According to the 68–95–99.7 Empirical Rule, approximately what percentage of bearings will have outer diameters within two standard deviations of the mean ($[70\text{ mm}, 130\text{ mm}]$)?

options.hint_markdown: Approximately $68\%$ of values lie within one standard deviation ($[\mu - \sigma, \mu + \sigma] = [85, 115]$), not two.
Approximately $99.7\%$ of values lie within three standard deviations ($[\mu - 3\sigma, \mu + 3\sigma] = [55, 145]$), not two.
The normal distribution has infinite support $(-\infty, +\infty)$, so no finite interval contains $100\%$ of the distribution.

stages.explanation_markdown: The Empirical Rule (68–95–99.7 rule) provides standard approximations for normal distributions: approximately $68\%$ of observations fall within $\pm 1\sigma$, approximately $95\%$ fall within $\pm 2\sigma$, and approximately $99.7\%$ fall within $\pm 3\sigma$.

stages.prompt_markdown: Using exact standard normal tables or software ($Z = \pm 2.00$, $\Phi(2.00) \approx 0.97725$), find the exact cumulative probability $P(70 < X < 130) = \Phi(2.00) - \Phi(-2.00)$. Enter as a decimal rounded to four decimal places.
stages.explanation_markdown: Standardizing the interval endpoints yields $Z_1 = \frac{70 - 100}{15} = -2.00$ and $Z_2 = \frac{130 - 100}{15} = +2.00$. From cumulative normal tables: $\Phi(2.00) \approx 0.97725$ and $\Phi(-2.00) \approx 0.02275$. The exact probability is $\Phi(2.00) - \Phi(-2.00) = 0.97725 - 0.02275 = 0.9545$ (or $95.45\%$). The Empirical Rule's "$95\%$" is a rounded rule of thumb. Excel formula: `=NORM.DIST(130, 100, 15, TRUE) - NORM.DIST(70, 100, 15, TRUE)` or `=NORM.S.DIST(2, TRUE) - NORM.S.DIST(-2, TRUE)`.

stages.prompt_markdown: Under what condition is the 68–95–99.7 Empirical Rule valid to use?

options.text_markdown: Only when the underlying distribution is unimodal, symmetric, and approximately bell-shaped (normal). For skewed or non-normal distributions, Chebyshev's inequality applies instead.
For all probability distributions regardless of shape, because every distribution with finite variance has a mean and standard deviation.
options.hint_markdown: For heavily skewed or bimodal distributions, the proportion within $2\sigma$ can differ drastically from $95\%$. Chebyshev guarantees at least $1 - 1/k^2 = 75\%$, not $95\%$.

options.text_markdown: Only for the standard normal distribution $Z \sim N(0, 1)$, not for general normal distributions with non-zero means.
options.hint_markdown: The Empirical Rule applies to any normal distribution $N(\mu, \sigma^2)$ because standardization transforms any normal variable into standard units.

options.text_markdown: Only for discrete distributions with integer counts.
options.hint_markdown: The Empirical Rule is derived from the continuous normal curve.

stages.explanation_markdown: The 68–95–99.7 rule is strictly valid only for approximately normal (bell-shaped, symmetric) distributions. For arbitrary or skewed distributions, Chebyshev's theorem guarantees at least $1 - 1/2^2 = 75\%$ of data within $2$ standard deviations, but cannot guarantee $\approx 95\%$.
